questions.question: How do you structure your time in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Evaluating whether the candidate can manage time effectively under pressure and prioritize design activities in a structured manner.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers spend 30 minutes writing perfect code for one class instead of showing the overall design first, leaving no time to discuss trade-offs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Verbally announce your time allocation at the start: 'I'll spend 5 minutes clarifying, then 10 on the class structure' — shows metacognitive awareness and planning ability.

questions.direct_answer: A 45-minute LLD interview should follow this rough allocation: 5 minutes to clarify requirements and scope, 5 minutes to identify core entities and relationships, 10 minutes to sketch a class diagram on the whiteboard, 15 minutes to write key Java class skeletons with method signatures, and 10 minutes to discuss design patterns, trade-offs, and extensibility.

items: Clarify first: nail the requirements before drawing anything
Identify entities before drawing: think on paper, not at the diagram
Draw high-level first: boxes and relationships, then fill detail
Write code for the most interesting class, not all classes
Save time for design discussion: patterns, trade-offs, extensions
Verbalize throughout: the interviewer follows your design as you explain

answer_sections.content: Time management in LLD is critical — 45 minutes goes fast. I spend the first 5 minutes clarifying requirements: what are the key use cases, any specific constraints? Then 5 minutes identifying entities — I list the nouns and verbs on a corner of the board. Then 10 minutes on the class diagram: all classes, relationships, and key methods. For the remaining 25 minutes, I write Java class skeletons for the 2-3 most interesting or complex classes — not all of them — and discuss design patterns I'm applying. The biggest mistake is spending 30 minutes perfecting the class diagram before writing any code. Interviewers want to see code, not just boxes.

How do you handle it if you realize mid-design that your initial approach was wrong?

speakable_v2.hook: Treat the 45 minutes like a budget: overspend on the diagram and you'll have nothing left for the code that proves you can build it.

beats.text: Time allocation is the most overlooked LLD skill. A structured split keeps you from over-investing in one phase and leaving interviewers without seeing your code.

groups.text: Write class skeletons for the 2 or 3 most interesting classes. Not all of them — the interviewer wants depth over breadth.

groups.heading: Minutes 35 to 45 — Discuss

sections.title: Structuring Your Time in an LLD Interview
sections.content:
A 45-minute LLD interview rewards **time discipline**. A workable budget: **5 min** clarify requirements, **5 min** identify entities and relationships, **10 min** sketch the class diagram, **15 min** write key Java skeletons with method signatures, **10 min** discuss patterns, trade-offs, and extensibility.

The most common failure is overspending on the diagram and leaving no time for code — interviewers want to see you turn boxes into actual classes. Keep a rough clock in your head and narrate as you go.

sections.content:
blue|0-5 min Clarify|~Scope first|key use cases|constraints|what's in/out
emerald|5-10 min Entities|~Noun-verb scan|candidate classes|actors|relationships
amber|10-20 min Diagram|~High-level first|boxes + key methods|relationship arrows|then fill detail
violet|20-35 min Code|~Depth over breadth|2-3 key classes|real signatures|not every class
rose|35-45 min Discuss|~Save time for this|patterns + trade-offs|extensibility|answer follow-ups

sections.title: The 45-Minute Budget
sections.content:
| Time | Phase | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 min | Clarify | Scope, constraints, in/out of scope |
| 5–10 min | Entities | Noun-verb analysis, actors, relationships |
| 10–20 min | Class diagram | Boxes, key fields/methods, arrows |
| 20–35 min | Java skeletons | Real classes, signatures, key methods |
| 35–45 min | Trade-offs | Patterns, extensibility, concurrency, Q&A |

sections.title: What the 'Skeleton' Phase Produces
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Over-drawing the diagram** — 20 minutes of boxes, no code. Cap the diagram.
- **Skipping clarification** to save time — you design the wrong thing faster.
- **Silent working** — narrate so the interviewer follows your reasoning.
- **No time for trade-offs** — leave the last 10 minutes for patterns and extensibility.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Budget: **5 clarify / 5 entities / 10 diagram / 15 code / 10 trade-offs**.
- **Cap the diagram** — code is what proves you can build it.
- Don't skip clarification, even under time pressure.
- **Narrate continuously** so the interviewer follows you.
- Reserve the final stretch for **trade-offs and extensibility**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I treat the forty-five minutes as a budget and keep a rough clock in my head. I spend the first five minutes clarifying — scope, constraints, what's explicitly in and out. The next five identifying the core entities and their relationships using noun-verb analysis. Then about ten minutes sketching the class diagram, with boxes, the key fields and methods, and the relationship arrows. The biggest chunk, around fifteen minutes, goes to writing key Java skeletons — turning the diagram boxes into actual classes with real method signatures. And I save the last ten minutes for discussing design patterns, trade-offs, extensibility, and answering follow-ups.

The single most common way people mismanage this is overspending on the diagram. It's tempting to make it perfect, but if you burn twenty minutes drawing boxes you've got nothing left to show you can actually translate that into code, and that's exactly what interviewers want to see. So I cap the diagram deliberately and move to skeletons. Under time pressure, signatures and relationships matter more than complete method bodies — I'll stub a method with a comment rather than implement every line.

The other thing I do throughout is narrate. I think out loud so the interviewer can follow my reasoning, because in a design interview the process is the product. And I never skip clarification to save time, because designing the wrong thing faster doesn't help anyone.

questions.question: What are the most common mistakes in LLD interviews and how do you avoid them?

interviewer_intent.testing: Assessing self-awareness about design pitfalls and whether the candidate has reflected on good LLD practices from study or mock interviews.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers memorize design patterns but don't understand when NOT to use them, leading to over-engineered solutions for simple problems.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention a specific mistake you made in a past mock interview and how you corrected it — shows growth mindset and learning from experience.

questions.direct_answer: Common LLD mistakes include jumping straight to coding without clarifying requirements, creating god classes that handle too many responsibilities violating SRP, forgetting to model enumerations for states and types, over-engineering with unnecessary patterns, and failing to articulate trade-offs. Avoid these by following a structured approach: clarify first, identify entities, model state machines, apply patterns only when justified, and always discuss alternatives.

items: No clarification: starting to design before fully understanding requirements
God class: ParkingLot that handles fees, tickets, display, everything
Missing enums: forgetting SpotType, VehicleType, OrderStatus
Wrong pattern: forcing a pattern where it doesn't fit naturally
No trade-off discussion: presenting design as perfect rather than discussing limitations
Only drawing, no code: interviewers want to see Java, not just boxes

answer_sections.content: The mistakes I've been most careful to avoid: jumping to design without requirements — I've seen people spend 20 minutes on a design and then realize they misunderstood the problem. Creating a god class that violates SRP — it's tempting to put everything in one class but SRP must be enforced. Forgetting state enumerations — SpotType, OrderStatus are central to the design and forgetting them makes the model incomplete. Forcing patterns — if I can't explain naturally why I'm using a pattern, I shouldn't use it. And only drawing diagrams without writing code — LLD interviews expect Java class skeletons with real method signatures, not just boxes.

beats.text: Most LLD interview failures come from a small set of recurring mistakes. Knowing them ahead of time is half the battle.

items: Starting without clarifying: designing for 20 minutes then realizing you misunderstood the problem
God class: ParkingLot that calculates fees, issues tickets, and updates displays — SRP violation
Missing enums: forgetting SpotType, VehicleType, OrderStatus makes the model incomplete
Forcing patterns: if you can't explain why you're using a pattern, don't use it
Only drawing diagrams: interviewers want Java class skeletons with real method signatures — not just boxes

beats.text: A God class is the most common mistake. It's tempting to add fee calculation to ParkingLot because it's convenient. Resist it — the moment you ask 'what would make this class change?' and get three answers, it needs to be split.

non-obvious: not discussing trade-offs. Presenting your design as perfect is a red flag. Every design has trade-offs — saying 'I chose Strategy here for extensibility, but the cost is more classes' sounds more credible than saying it's the ideal solution.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Five classic mistakes; **four happen before you code**.
- **Clarify first** — never design the wrong thing fast.
- Split **God classes** by responsibility (SRP).
- Model states/types with **enums**, not strings.
- **Articulate trade-offs** — that's what 'standing out' looks like.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
From watching these interviews, the failures cluster into five mistakes, and what's striking is that four of them happen before you write any code. The first is jumping straight to coding without clarifying requirements, which means you might design the wrong system very efficiently. I avoid it by spending the first few minutes asking scope questions. The second is the God class — one giant class that parks vehicles, calculates fees, prints tickets, and sends notifications all at once. It violates Single Responsibility and is impossible to test, so I split it into focused classes, each with one reason to change.

The third is forgetting to use enums for states and types. Modelling vehicle type or order status as strings is fragile — typos compile and fail at runtime — so I reach for enums, which are type-safe and can carry behaviour. The fourth is over-engineering: layering on patterns nobody asked for, which adds complexity instead of value. Patterns should solve a real problem, not decorate the design. And the fifth is failing to articulate trade-offs.

That last one is really how you stand out. When I pick a HashMap over a TreeMap, or composition over inheritance, I say why out loud — what I'm optimising for and what I'm giving up. Interviewers can't read your mind, so the reasoning is as valuable as the result. The thread through all five fixes is a calm, structured approach: clarify, identify entities, assign responsibilities, model states, and narrate your decisions.

sections.title: Why the mistake happens
sections.content:
When you're uncertain about a design choice, present both options with their trade-offs and either ask for the interviewer's guidance or make an explicit choice while acknowledging the alternative.

For example: 'I could use a HashMap for constant-time lookups or a TreeMap for sorted access.

Most LLD interview failures cluster into five recurring mistakes: **jumping to code** without clarifying, building **God classes** that violate SRP, **forgetting enums** for states and types, **over-engineering** with needless patterns, and **failing to articulate trade-offs**. The fix is a structured approach: clarify first, identify entities, give each class one job, model states with enums, and verbalise *why* you chose each design. Notice that four of the five mistakes happen *before* the first line of code.

Common LLD mistakes include jumping straight to coding without clarifying requirements, creating god classes that handle too many responsibilities violating SRP, forgetting to model enumerations for states and types, over-engineering with unnecessary patterns, and failing to articulate trade-offs. Avoid these by following a structured approach: clarify first, identify entities, model state machines, apply patterns only when justified, and always discuss alternatives.

sections.content:

emerald|God class|~SRP violation|one class does it all|3+ reasons to change|split by responsibility

sections.title: The God class mistake
Split by responsibility (SRP)
sections.content:
```java
class ParkingLot     { Optional<ParkingTicket> park(Vehicle v); } // coordination
class FeeCalculator  { BigDecimal calculate(ParkingTicket t); }   // pricing
class TicketPrinter  { String format(ParkingTicket t); }          // presentation
class NotificationService { void sendSms(String to, String msg); } // notifications
```
*Each class has one reason to change and can be tested in isolation.*

sections.title: The Five Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Coding before clarifying** — you build the wrong thing. Ask scope questions first.
- **God classes** — split by responsibility (SRP).
- **No enums for states/types** — stringly-typed code is bug-prone; use enums.
- **Over-engineering** — patterns you don't need add complexity, not value.
- **No trade-off talk** — say why you chose HashMap over TreeMap, composition over inheritance.

questions.question: What should you say when you're not sure about a design decision in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Evaluating intellectual honesty, structured thinking under ambiguity, and whether you treat design as a conversation with stakeholders rather than a solo exam.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers either freeze and stop talking when uncertain, or fake confidence and charge ahead with a questionable choice, both showing poor judgment and inability to reason about trade-offs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame uncertainty as a question about priorities or constraints: 'This depends on whether read latency or memory footprint is more critical — what's the typical load pattern here?' shows you're thinking in terms of real-world trade-offs.

questions.direct_answer: When you're uncertain about a design choice, present both options with their trade-offs and either ask for the interviewer's guidance or make an explicit choice while acknowledging the alternative. For example: 'I could use a HashMap for constant-time lookups or a TreeMap for sorted access. I'll go with HashMap since spot retrieval seems more frequent than sorted iteration, but I'd benchmark in production.' This shows decision-making transparency and collaborative problem-solving.

answer_sections.content: When I face a design decision I'm unsure about, I present the trade-off explicitly. 'I'm considering two approaches: using an abstract Vehicle class which gives shared code but tighter inheritance coupling, versus an interface which is more flexible. For this parking lot, since the vehicles genuinely share attributes like licensePlate, I'll go with abstract class.' This shows design thinking even when uncertain. If I genuinely don't know, I say so: 'I'm not sure of the best pattern here — my instinct is Strategy, but I'm open to your guidance.' Interviewers often prefer a candidate who reasons through decisions honestly over one who makes confident-sounding choices without justification. Design is always about trade-offs, not perfect answers.

follow_up_questions: How do you communicate design uncertainty without seeming unprepared?
Is it better to make a decision and move on or discuss trade-offs extensively?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: "I don't know" sinks you; "here are two options and the trade-off, I'll go with this" is what they're actually scoring.

beats.text: Every LLD has design decisions with no perfect answer. How you handle uncertainty tells the interviewer more about your maturity than the decision itself.

items: Name both options: 'I could use abstract class or interface here'
State the trade-off: 'abstract class gives shared code but limits multiple inheritance; interface is more flexible'
Make a decision with a reason: 'since vehicles genuinely share attributes, I'll use abstract class'
Invite guidance if genuinely unsure: 'my instinct is Strategy here, but I'm open to your perspective'

beats.text: Instead of saying 'I'll use a Strategy pattern' with no explanation, say: 'I'm using Strategy for FeeCalculator because pricing rules change independently of the parking flow — that's the reason, not just the pattern name.'

non-obvious: interviewers often prefer a candidate who reasons through a trade-off honestly over one who makes confident-sounding choices without justification. Design is always about trade-offs — presenting it that way is a sign of experience.

speakable_v2.cap: Name options, state trade-offs, make a decision, give the reason. If you're genuinely unsure, say so and invite guidance. Honest reasoning beats confident bluffing.

sections.title: What to Say When You're Unsure
sections.content:
Uncertainty isn't a failure — *how you handle it* is being scored. When you're unsure of a design choice, **present both options with their trade-offs** and then either ask for the interviewer's steer or **make an explicit, reasoned choice** while acknowledging the alternative.

Example: *"I could use a `HashMap` for O(1) lookup or a `TreeMap` for sorted iteration. Lookups dominate here, so I'll go with `HashMap`, but I'd revisit if we needed ordered traversal."* That shows judgement under ambiguity — exactly what's tested.

sections.title: Handling Uncertainty
sections.content:
blue|Name both options|~Don't freeze|HashMap or TreeMap?|abstract or interface?|two reasonable choices
emerald|State the trade-off|~Cost vs benefit|O(1) vs sorted order|flexible vs shared code|make it explicit
amber|Decide with a reason|~Commit, in context|lookups dominate -> HashMap|note when you'd revisit|don't endlessly hedge
rose|Bluffing or freezing|~The wrong moves|fake confidence|silent picking|honest reasoning wins

sections.title: Java — Decide Out Loud with Trade-offs
The Uncertainty Playbook
sections.content:
| Step | What to say |
|---|---|
| 1 | "There are two reasonable options here…" |
| 2 | State each with its trade-off (cost/benefit) |
| 3 | Make an explicit choice and justify it for this context |
| 4 | Acknowledge when you'd revisit the decision |
| 5 | Optionally invite the interviewer's input |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Freezing or saying just "I don't know"** — show your reasoning instead.
- **Picking silently** — verbalise the alternatives and the trade-off.
- **Bluffing certainty** — false confidence is worse than honest reasoning.
- **Never deciding** — endless hedging reads as inability to commit; choose and justify.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Uncertainty is normal — **how you reason** is what's scored.
- Present **both options + trade-offs**, then choose explicitly.
- Justify the choice **for this context** and note when you'd revisit.
- Don't **bluff** certainty or **freeze**.
- Optionally invite the interviewer's steer.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When I'm unsure about a design decision, I treat it as a chance to show my reasoning rather than something to hide. The worst things I can do are freeze, just say I don't know, or bluff false confidence — all three read badly. Instead, I lay out the options. I'll say something like, there are two reasonable choices here, and walk through each with its trade-off.

A concrete example: if I'm choosing a data structure for spot lookup, I'd say I could use a HashMap for constant-time lookups, or a TreeMap if I need sorted iteration. Then I make an explicit, reasoned choice for this context — lookups are far more frequent than sorted traversal here, so I'll go with HashMap — and I acknowledge the alternative and when I'd revisit it, like if a requirement for ordered traversal showed up. That whole move demonstrates judgement under ambiguity, which is exactly what the interviewer is scoring.

Sometimes it's also fine, after laying out the trade-offs, to ask the interviewer whether they have a preference, especially if the choice depends on a requirement we haven't pinned down. That's collaborative, not weak. The one thing I avoid is endless hedging without committing, because never deciding looks like an inability to make a call. So the pattern is: name the options, state the trade-offs, commit with a reason, and stay open to changing my mind. Honest, structured reasoning beats fake certainty every time.

questions.question: How do you handle extended or follow-up requirements in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Assessing whether you designed with the Open-Closed Principle in mind from the start and can extend functionality without breaking existing code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers immediately modify existing classes by adding if-else branches or flags like isElectric, which creates fragile code that violates the Open-Closed Principle.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point to a specific abstraction you built earlier that now enables clean extension: 'I used ParkingSpot as an abstract class so adding ElectricSpot just means one new subclass with a chargingRate field'.

questions.direct_answer: When the interviewer adds a new requirement like 'support electric vehicle charging spots', extend your design using abstraction rather than modifying existing code. Introduce a new subclass like ElectricChargingSpot or add a capability interface. If your initial design doesn't accommodate this cleanly, acknowledge the limitation honestly and explain what refactoring you'd do to make it extensible.

answer_sections.content: When an interviewer adds a follow-up requirement, I treat it as an OCP test. 'Now add electric vehicle charging spots' — I extend without modifying: add ElectricVehicle extends Vehicle, add CHARGING SpotType to the enum, add ChargingSpot extends ParkingSpot. None of the existing code changes. If the requirement truly requires changing existing classes, I acknowledge it: 'This would require modifying the FeeCalculator interface, which suggests my initial design should have used a more flexible approach from the start. Here's how I'd refactor it...' Showing that you can extend AND knowing when to refactor demonstrates design maturity. Never pretend your design handles everything perfectly from the start.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: A good follow-up isn't an attack — it's the interviewer checking whether your design was open for extension all along.

beats.text: Follow-up requirements are a deliberate OCP test. The interviewer wants to see whether you can extend your design cleanly or whether you need to rewrite it.

items: Identify what's new: is it a new type, a new behavior, or a new flow?
Extend without modifying: add a new subclass, enum value, or strategy implementation
If modification is unavoidable, acknowledge it: say how you'd refactor and why your initial design could have been more flexible
Never pretend your design handles everything perfectly — that's a red flag

beats.text: Add EV charging spots: ElectricVehicle extends Vehicle, add CHARGING to SpotType enum, add ChargingSpot extends ParkingSpot. None of the existing code changes. That's OCP — and it's the answer the interviewer is looking for.

non-obvious: if the new requirement genuinely breaks your design, say so cleanly: 'This would require changing the FeeCalculator interface — my initial design should have used a more extensible approach. Here's how I'd refactor.' Showing you can recognize and articulate design debt is a strength, not a weakness.

speakable_v2.cap: Treat follow-ups as OCP tests. Extend with new classes first. If you must modify, acknowledge the trade-off and show the refactor. Never bluff.

sections.title: Handling Follow-Up Requirements
sections.content:
Mid-interview, the interviewer will add a requirement — *"now support electric-vehicle charging spots"*. The graceful response is to **extend through abstraction**, not rewrite: add a subclass (`ElectricChargingSpot`) or a capability interface, leaving existing classes untouched. That's the **Open/Closed Principle** in live action.

If your original design *can't* absorb the change cleanly, **say so honestly** and describe the refactor you'd do. Interviewers value an honest "my current design assumed X; I'd introduce an interface here" far more than a forced hack.

sections.title: Follow-Ups Are an OCP Test
sections.content:
blue|Restate the ask|~Confirm understanding|"support EV charging"|scope the change|new type or behaviour?
emerald|Extend, don't edit|~Open/Closed|new subclass|new interface|existing code untouched
amber|If it can't absorb it|~Be honest|name the limitation|describe the refactor|beats an ugly hack
rose|Pitfalls|~Read as immature|hacking into classes|pretending it fits|silent rewriting

sections.title: Extend, don't rewrite
Follow-Up Response Playbook
sections.content:
| Step | What to say/do |
|---|---|
| 1 | Restate the new requirement to confirm understanding |
| 2 | Check if existing abstractions absorb it (subclass/interface) |
| 3 | If yes: extend via new class — narrate the OCP win |
| 4 | If no: name the limitation honestly + describe the refactor |
| 5 | Note any trade-off the change introduces |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Hacking it into existing classes** — editing working code instead of extending it.
- **Pretending the design handles it** when it doesn't — interviewers see through this.
- **Silent rewriting** — narrate what you're changing and why.
- **Ignoring trade-offs** the new requirement introduces (e.g. extra state, sync needs).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Extend through abstraction** (subclass/interface), not by editing working code (OCP).
- If the design can't absorb it, **say so honestly** + describe the refactor.
- **Restate** the requirement first to confirm understanding.
- **Narrate** the change and its trade-offs.
- Follow-ups test whether your design was **open for extension**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When the interviewer adds a requirement mid-stream — say, now support electric-vehicle charging spots — I see it as a test of whether my design was open for extension, not as an attack. So my first move is to restate the requirement to make sure I understood it. Then I check whether my existing abstractions can absorb it. Ideally I can add a new subclass like ElectricChargingSpot, or a capability interface like Chargeable, and leave all the existing classes untouched. That's the Open/Closed Principle in action, and I'd narrate it: I'm adding a new class rather than editing working code, so nothing that already works can break.

The more interesting case is when my original design can't absorb the change cleanly. The wrong response is to hack it into existing classes or pretend the design already handles it — interviewers see straight through that. The right response is to be honest: I'd say something like, my current design assumed all spots are passive, so to support charging I'd introduce a Chargeable interface here and refactor these two classes. Naming the limitation and describing the refactor demonstrates more maturity than forcing an ugly workaround.

And whatever I do, I narrate it and I call out any trade-off the new requirement introduces — extra state to manage, new concurrency concerns, more complexity. Showing that I can evolve a design gracefully, and that I know when evolution requires a small refactor, is exactly what the follow-up is probing for.

questions.question: How do you demonstrate that you understand SOLID principles in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Assessing whether the candidate understands SOLID as practical design heuristics that emerge naturally, not just as acronyms to memorize and recite.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers mention SOLID by name ('I'm using SRP here') without actually showing the problem it solves or the design smell it prevents.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a violation first, then fix it: 'This ParkingLotManager is doing too much, let me split out the payment logic' — teaching while designing.

questions.direct_answer: Demonstrate SOLID by applying principles naturally during design, not as a checklist. Show SRP by splitting a god class into focused responsibilities. Show OCP by using interfaces so new vehicle types don't modify existing code. Show LSP by ensuring subclasses like Motorcycle can replace Vehicle without breaking logic. Show ISP with small interfaces like Payable instead of one giant IVehicle. Show DIP by depending on abstractions like PaymentProcessor interface, not concrete CreditCardProcessor.

items: SRP: 'I'm separating FeeCalculator because it has a different reason to change'
OCP: 'Adding a new vehicle type doesn't require changing ParkingLot — it extends Vehicle'
LSP: 'Car and Motorcycle both implement Vehicle correctly — they're interchangeable'
ISP: 'Separate Payable and Reservable interfaces — not everything can do both'
DIP: 'ParkingLot depends on IFeeCalculator, not HourlyFeeCalculator specifically'

answer_sections.content: The best way to demonstrate SOLID is to apply it naturally in your design narrative, not recite the acronym. When I create a FeeCalculator class, I say 'I'm putting the pricing logic here rather than in ParkingLot, because pricing has its own reason to change — that's SRP.' When I use an interface: 'I'm depending on FeeCalculator as an interface so ParkingLot doesn't need to know whether we're using hourly or daily pricing — that's DIP.' When I add ElectricVehicle: 'We can extend the vehicle hierarchy without modifying ParkingLot — that's OCP.' Weaving these principles into your design explanation shows fluency rather than recitation.

speakable_v2.hook: Don't announce 'now I'll demonstrate SOLID' — let each principle fall naturally out of a decision you're already explaining.

beats.text: The best way to show SOLID is to weave it into your design narrative — not recite the acronym when asked. Apply each principle as you make each design decision.

groups.heading: SRP — say it while splitting classes
groups.text: 'I'm creating FeeCalculator as a separate class because pricing has its own reason to change — that's SRP.'

groups.heading: OCP — say it when adding abstractions
groups.text: 'Adding ElectricVehicle doesn't require changing ParkingLot — we extend without modifying. That's OCP.'

groups.heading: LSP — say it about subclasses
groups.text: 'Car and Motorcycle both implement Vehicle correctly — anywhere we use a Vehicle reference, either works. That's LSP.'

groups.heading: ISP — say it when creating interfaces
groups.text: 'I'm using separate Payable and Reservable interfaces — not everything can do both. That's ISP.'

groups.heading: DIP — say it about dependencies
groups.text: 'ParkingLot depends on FeeCalculator as an interface, not HourlyFeeCalculator specifically. That's DIP.'

beats.text: candidates miss: waiting for the interviewer to ask about SOLID. The fluent approach is to name each principle naturally as you apply it. That shows the principle guides your thinking — not just your recitation.

speakable_v2.cap: Don't recite SOLID — apply it and name it as you go. 'I'm doing this because of SRP' is worth ten times more than listing the acronym at the end.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Apply SOLID as **natural design moves**, then name the principle.
- SRP (split), OCP (interface to extend), LSP (substitutable subtypes).
- ISP (small interfaces), DIP (inject abstractions).
- Don't **recite** or **announce** — demonstrate.
- Use the principles the **problem calls for**, not all five forced in.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The key to demonstrating SOLID is to apply each principle as a natural part of designing, and only name it after I've made the move — that reads as genuine fluency rather than reciting flashcards. So when I split a class that was doing too much into a FeeCalculator and a ParkingSpot, I'll say I'm separating these so each has a single reason to change — that's Single Responsibility. When I introduce an interface so that adding a new vehicle type doesn't require editing existing code, I'll note that keeps the design open for extension but closed for modification, which is Open/Closed.

For Liskov Substitution, I make sure a subtype like Motorcycle can stand in for Vehicle anywhere without breaking logic — no method that throws unexpectedly — and I'll call that out if it's relevant. For Interface Segregation, I prefer small focused interfaces like Parkable or Payable over one giant IVehicle that forces classes to implement methods they don't need. And for Dependency Inversion, I inject a FeeCalculator interface into the ParkingLot through its constructor, so the high-level class depends on an abstraction rather than a concrete implementation.

The mistake I avoid is announcing up front that I'm going to demonstrate SOLID, or reciting the five principles like a list. Interviewers will probe whether my design actually matches my words, so I let the principles fall out of decisions I'm already explaining, and I only invoke the ones the problem genuinely calls for rather than forcing all five.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
When you're uncertain about a design choice, present both options with their trade-offs and either ask for the interviewer's guidance or make an explicit choice while acknowledging the alternative.

For example: 'I could use a HashMap for constant-time lookups or a TreeMap for sorted access.

I'll go with HashMap since spot retrieval seems more frequent than sorted iteration, but I'd benchmark in production.' This shows decision-making transparency and collaborative problem-solving.

Common LLD mistakes include jumping straight to coding without clarifying requirements, creating god classes that handle too many responsibilities violating SRP, forgetting to model enumerations for states and types, over-engineering with unnecessary patterns, and failing to articulate trade-offs. Avoid these by following a structured approach: clarify first, identify entities, model state machines, apply patterns only when justified, and always discuss alternatives.

sections.title: Java — SOLID Falling Out of Decisions
Make the Move, Then Name It
sections.content:
amber|Split the God class|~SRP|one job per class|FeeCalculator vs Spot|"one reason to change"
blue|Interface for new types|~OCP|add, don't edit|new Strategy|"open for extension"
emerald|Subtypes behave|~LSP|no surprise throws|Motorcycle is-a Vehicle|"substitutable"
violet|Small interfaces|~ISP|Payable not IVehicle|implement what you need|"no fat interface"
rose|Inject abstractions|~DIP|constructor injection|FeeCalculator|"depend on contracts"

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reciting SOLID as a list** — apply it; name it only after the move.
- **Announcing patterns/principles upfront** — let them emerge from decisions.
- **Claiming a principle you didn't apply** — interviewers probe; match words to design.
- **Forcing all five** — use the ones the problem actually calls for.
